extracted.intended_audience: young writers (including scientists) pitching op-eds / op-ed competition entrants
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writing opinion essays (op-eds) and pitching them to publications, with special notes for scientists and young/first-time pitchers. Covers what makes an op-ed effective and how to craft a successful pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a topic you are passionate about
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important starting point for an op-ed is finding a topic that you are passionate about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion helps produce strong, authentic takes; passion underlies compelling worldview and voice. (Original wording: 'The most important starting point for an op-ed is finding a topic that you are passionate about.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Give insight into the writer's worldview
rubrics_metrics.description: Op-eds should give the reader insight into a writer's worldview; by the end of the essay the reader should feel they have a good understanding of how the writer thinks and what they are passionate about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Francisco J. Rivera Rosario explicitly looks for pieces that reveal the author's perspective: 'I'm looking for op-eds that give me insight into a writer's worldview... By the end of the essay, I want to feel like I have a good understanding of how they think.' Use the piece to show thinking and priorities, not just facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be brief
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity makes op-eds appealing to a large portion of readers; keep writing concise and focused. (Original phrasing: 'Good op-eds are brief, direct, and unwavering in their convictions.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Be direct and have an unwavering conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Op-eds should be direct and unwavering in their convictions — clearly state your position and argue it with conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directness and a firm stance make an op-ed persuasive and accessible; avoid wishy-washy or hedged language. (Original phrasing included as above.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate ideas clearly to your target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure you communicate ideas clearly to your target audience; clarity of communication is a key editorial concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors act as sounding boards to help writers shape ambitious takes and 'ensure they communicate these ideas clearly to their target audience.' Tailor language, explanation, and examples to the readership of the outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use op-eds to explain science, change narratives, or advocate
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientist-written op-eds: use the form to communicate scientific concepts to the public, seek to change narratives, focus on public outreach and advocacy, or explain why science matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Fonna Forman's piece on climate education and Nicole Rust's essay on scientists doing public outreach. Op-eds can translate complex ideas into accessible arguments and shift public conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize with life experience when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Op-eds can be personal essays that highlight how a writer's work shapes their life experiences, humanizing the subject and showing its emotional impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal stories to make abstract or technical topics resonant for general readers, as in Ida Momennejad's piece about neuroscience and personal grief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and follow editorial guidelines of the publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Before pitching, make sure you read the editorial guidelines of the publication you're pitching to; these provide clear directions about what the publication is looking for in a pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most publications post guidelines on their websites; following them increases the chance your pitch will be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure your pitch is a good fit for the publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Be very familiar with what the publication publishes; many pitches fail because they are not right for that specific publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immerse yourself in the publication's writing to confirm fit. Editors receive many pitches that are solid but mismatched—avoid that by matching tone, subject, and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate for yourself in the pitch: explain why you are the right person
rubrics_metrics.description: Your pitch needs to be well-researched and have a solid premise, and you should tell editors why you are the right person to write the piece — be confident and explain how your life experiences make you uniquely equipped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine a clear, researched idea with a concise explanation of your authority or unique perspective; confidence in the pitch helps persuade editors to commission or accept the piece.
